THE NIGHT THAT LORCA COMES SHALL BE A STRANGE NIGHT IN THE SOUTH, IT SHALL BE THE TIME WHEN NEGROES LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, GREEN TRAINS SHALL ARRIVE FROM RED PLANET MARS CRACKLING BLUENESS SHALL SEND TOOTH-COVERED CARS FOR THEM TO LEAVE IN, TO GO INTO THE NORTH FOREVER, AND I SEE MY LITTLE GIRL MOTHER AGAIN WITH HER CROSS THAT IS NOT BURNING, HER SKIRTS OF BLACK, OF ALL COLORS, HER AURA OF FAMILIARITY. THE SOUTH SHALL WEEP BITTER TEARS TO NO AVAIL, THE NEGROES HAVE GONE INTO CRACKLING BLUENESS. CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL ARRIVE WITH THE BOSTON COMMONS, TO TAKE ELISSI LANDI NORTH, CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL BE LAYING ON BOSTON COMMONS, ELISSI LANDI SHALL FEEL ALIVE AGAIN. I SHALL CALL HER NAME AS SHE STEPS ON TO THE BOSTON COMMONS, AND FLIES NORTH FOREVER, LINCOLN SHALL BE THERE, TO SEE THEM LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, ELISSI LANDI, SHE WILL BE GREEN. THE WHITE SOUTH SHALL GATHER AT PRESERVATION HALL.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: THE, NIGHT, THAT

outputs.L1:
The night that Lorca comes shall be a strange night in the South—it shall be the hour when the Negroes depart the South forever. Green trains shall arrive from the red planet Mars, and a crackling blueness shall dispatch tooth-covered cars in which they may take their leave, journeying into the North for all time. And I behold once more my little girl-mother, bearing her cross that does not burn, her skirts of black and of every color, her aura of tender familiarity. The South shall weep bitter tears, yet all in vain, for the Negroes have vanished into the crackling blueness.

Crispus Attucks shall arrive with the Boston Commons to bear Elissi Landi northward; Crispus Attucks shall lie upon the Boston Commons, and Elissi Landi shall feel alive once again. I shall call her name as she steps onto the Boston Commons and takes flight into the North forever. Lincoln shall be present there, to witness their eternal departure from the South. Elissi Landi—she shall be green. And the white South shall gather at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L2: When Lorca arrives, that evening will be unlike any other in the South—it will mark the moment when Black people depart from the region for good. Green locomotives will roll in from crimson Mars, and a crackling shade of blue will dispatch tooth-lined vehicles to carry them away, northward and never returning. And once more I glimpse my young mother, her cross unlit, wearing her black skirts of every hue, surrounded by her familiar glow. The South will shed its bitter tears in vain, for the Black people have vanished into that crackling blue. Crispus Attucks will come bearing the Boston Commons, meaning to bring Elissi Landi to the North; Crispus Attucks will stretch out upon the Boston Commons, and Elissi Landi will once again know the feeling of life. I will speak her name aloud as she moves onto the Boston Commons and soars northward eternally, and Lincoln will stand watching as they abandon the South forever. Elissi Landi—she will turn green. Meanwhile, the white South will assemble together at Preservation Hall.

# The Night of Departure

The arrival of Lorca heralds a strange and transformative night across the South—a night unlike any other, when Black people will finally depart the region forever. His coming signals not merely a change but a rupture, a moment when the ordinary laws of the world seem to bend and give way to something extraordinary.

The means of this great departure are rendered in surreal, otherworldly imagery. Green trains descend from Mars, and a crackling blueness fills the air, becoming the impossible vehicles by which the migration north takes place. These are not the ordinary trains of the Great Migration but something dreamlike and cosmic, suggesting that this exodus transcends the boundaries of the physical world altogether.

Within this fantastical landscape, the speaker envisions a deeply personal moment: a reunion with his young mother. She appears before him accompanied by a non-burning cross—an image that inverts the terror of the burning crosses that once haunted the South—and surrounded by an aura of warmth and familiarity. In this vision, the instruments of hatred are transformed, stripped of their power to harm, and what remains is tenderness and recognition.

To witness and facilitate this exodus, historical figures emerge from the past. Crispus Attucks, the first to fall in the American Revolution, and Abraham Lincoln, the Great Emancipator, appear as guardians of the journey. Their presence links this surreal departure to the enduring themes of freedom and liberation, situating the night's events within the long historical struggle for Black emancipation.

As the Black population vanishes into the crackling blueness, the White South is left behind to weep in vain. They gather at Preservation Hall—a name heavy with irony—clinging to a heritage and a way of life that is slipping irretrievably from their grasp. Their tears accomplish nothing; the departure is complete, and what they sought to preserve has finally, irrevocably, gone.

# The Great Departure: A Reading

This surrealist poem transforms the historical reality of Black migration from the American South into a cosmic, apocalyptic vision. Rather than depicting the movement through conventional realism, the poet reaches for the fantastical—green trains descending from Mars, a crackling blueness charging the atmosphere—to capture the enormity of what such an exodus truly means. This is not merely a physical relocation but a rupture in the fabric of reality itself, a moment when the ordinary laws of the world seem suspended.

The imagery works to defamiliarize the familiar. By rendering the trains as otherworldly vessels arriving from another planet, the poem suggests that liberation, when it finally comes, will feel like something from beyond human experience. The "crackling blueness" electrifies the scene with tension and possibility, an almost supernatural charge signaling that the world is about to change irrevocably. These surreal elements do not distance us from the poem's emotional truth; instead, they amplify it, insisting that the weight of centuries cannot be conveyed through plain description alone.

Threaded through this dreamlike landscape are historical figures who anchor the vision in a genuine reckoning with the past. Crispus Attucks—among the first to die in the American Revolution, a Black man who bled for a nation that would not grant his people freedom—stands as an emblem of sacrifice unrepaid. Lincoln appears as a figure bound up with the promise and the betrayal of emancipation. Their presence transforms the poem into a conversation across time, summoning the dead to witness the departure of the living. The past is not settled; it walks alongside the present, demanding acknowledgment.

The poem returns again and again to three interwoven motifs. **Departure** dominates as an image of finality: the people are leaving the South *forever*, severing themselves from the land that held both their suffering and their history. **Transformation** accompanies this leaving, as the surreal imagery suggests that those who go are not merely changing address but changing state of being—becoming something new, shedding the identities imposed upon them. And **reunion** offers a redemptive counterpoint, gathering the scattered and the dead, the living and the remembered, into a single visionary community.

Together, these motifs elevate the poem beyond a document of migration into a meditation on racial liberation and historical justice. The exodus becomes an act of collective self-reclamation, a refusal to remain within a geography and a history defined by oppression. Yet the poem does not simply celebrate escape. By invoking memory and the dead, it insists that freedom must carry the past with it—that liberation is inseparable from remembrance. The enduring legacy of oppression cannot be outrun; it can only be reckoned with, carried forward, and ultimately transformed.

In this way, the poem achieves its visionary power. It fuses the concrete and the cosmic, the historical and the surreal, to render an event that is at once specific to the Black American experience and mythic in its scope. The result is a work that gives full weight to freedom, memory, and the long shadow of injustice—imagining not just a departure from a place, but a passage toward a wholly reimagined world.
outputs.L5:
# The Night That Changed Everything

There are moments in life that divide time into before and after. For me, it was the night that everything shifted—quietly, without warning, yet with a force that reshaped who I would become.

## The Setting

It was an ordinary evening at first. The sky had darkened into a deep velvet blue, and the streetlights flickered on one by one. The night carried that particular stillness that makes the world feel both smaller and infinitely vast at the same time. I remember thinking how peaceful everything seemed, unaware of what was about to unfold.

## The Turning Point

The night that I speak of arrived without fanfare. A single phone call, a chance encounter, a decision made in a heartbeat—sometimes the largest changes hinge on the smallest of moments. I stood at the window, watching the darkness, and felt the weight of a choice pressing against my chest.

The thing about the night is that it strips away distractions. In the silence, our thoughts grow louder, and the truths we avoid during the day finally demand to be heard. That was exactly what happened. Everything I had been running from caught up with me.

## The Reflection

Looking back now, I understand that the night that once frightened me was actually a gift. It taught me that growth often comes cloaked in darkness, and that the moments we least expect can hold the greatest meaning.

The night ended, as all nights do, giving way to a hesitant dawn. But the person who greeted that morning was not the same one who had watched the stars the evening before. That is the power of a single night—the power to transform, to reveal, and ultimately, to renew.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, apocalyptic prose poem in all capital letters about the day Federico García Lorca arrives and Black people leave the South forever, using imagery of green Mars trains, crackling blueness, Crispus Attucks, Boston Commons, Lincoln, and Preservation Hall.
counterfactuals.output:
THE DAY LORCA CAME AND THE SOUTH EMPTIED OF US

THE MORNING BROKE OPEN LIKE A POMEGRANATE FULL OF FLIES AND FEDERICO GARCÍA LORCA STEPPED DOWN FROM A GREEN MARS TRAIN THAT HAD NO ENGINE ONLY THE MEMORY OF SPAIN BLEEDING THROUGH ITS WINDOWS. HE WORE THE MOON LIKE A COLLAR. HE CARRIED THE DUENDE IN A PAPER SACK AND WHEN HE OPENED IT THE COTTON FIELDS BEGAN TO SCREAM IN CRACKLING BLUENESS.

AND WE LEFT. ALL OF US. WE LEFT THE SOUTH FOREVER ON THAT DAY OF SMOKE AND SAPPHIRE, OUR FEET NO LONGER TOUCHING THE RED DIRT THAT REMEMBERED OUR GRANDMOTHERS, OUR FEET RISING INTO THE ELECTRIC AIR WHERE CRISPUS ATTUCKS WALKED AHEAD OF US WITH FIVE BULLETS STILL SINGING IN HIS CHEST LIKE FIVE BLACK STARS, LIKE FIVE MOUTHS SPEAKING THE FIRST WORD OF THE REVOLUTION THAT NEVER FINISHED ITS SENTENCE.

THE GREEN MARS TRAINS MULTIPLIED ACROSS THE SKY. THEY RAN ON RAILS OF LIGHTNING TOWARD BOSTON COMMONS WHERE THE GRASS WAS THE COLOR OF DROWNED TRUMPETS. FEDERICO SANG A DEEP SONG, A CANTE JONDO SO OLD IT PREDATED SORROW, AND THE MAGNOLIAS TURNED TO ASH, AND THE PLANTATIONS FOLDED THEMSELVES INTO ORIGAMI GHOSTS AND FLOATED OFF INTO THE CRACKLING BLUENESS OF A GOD WHO HAD FINALLY DECIDED TO PAY ATTENTION.

LINCOLN ROSE FROM HIS MARBLE CHAIR. HIS STONE EYES WEPT MERCURY. HE WALKED WITH US THOUGH HE COULD NOT KEEP UP, HIS GRAY BODY CRUMBLING INTO PIGEONS, HIS PROCLAMATION UNSPOOLING FROM HIS MOUTH LIKE A TONGUE OF WOUNDED PAPER, AND FEDERICO CAUGHT IT AND READ IT ALOUD IN ANDALUSIAN SPANISH AND SOMEHOW WE UNDERSTOOD EVERY BROKEN PROMISE INSIDE IT.

WE MARCHED. WE MARCHED THROUGH THE APOCALYPSE OF OUR OWN LEAVING. BEHIND US THE SOUTH BECAME A PHOTOGRAPH OF ITSELF, THEN THE ASHES OF A PHOTOGRAPH, THEN NOTHING BUT THE HUM OF CICADAS PLAYING A FUNERAL IN A KEY NO PIANO EVER OWNED.

AND AT THE END OF THE WORLD THERE WAS PRESERVATION HALL. THE ONLY BUILDING LEFT STANDING. THE OLD MEN INSIDE STILL PLAYING, THEIR CLARINETS FULL OF HURRICANE, THEIR CORNETS FULL OF SAINTS, AND WHEN FEDERICO ENTERED WITH HIS PAPER SACK OF DUENDE THE MUSIC ROSE UP GREEN AND MARTIAN AND CRACKLING AND BLUE, AND CRISPUS ATTUCKS TOOK UP THE DRUM, AND LINCOLN'S PIGEONS CIRCLED THE CEILING LIKE A HALO OF THE UNFORGIVEN, AND WE DANCED.

WE DANCED INTO THE NEXT COUNTRY.
WE DANCED OUT OF HISTORY.
WE LEFT THE SOUTH FOREVER AND THE SOUTH DID NOT DESERVE OUR GOODBYE, ONLY OUR MUSIC, ONLY THE LAST BLUE NOTE HANGING IN THE AIR LIKE A NOOSE UNTYING ITSELF, LIKE A THROAT REMEMBERING HOW TO BREATHE, LIKE MARS PULLING ITS GREEN TRAINS HOME.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental beat-poetry in the style of Bob Kaufman, filled with jazz surrealism, racial imagery, and dreamlike repetition about an exodus from the South.
counterfactuals.output:
**Exodus in Blue Minor**

*(for the ones who walked out of the burning alphabet)*

I

They packed the moon into a cardboard valise
and left the South wearing its cotton crown of thorns,
left the mules dreaming in the ledger of God,
left the porches muttering their brown hymns to no one,
no one, no one but the crows keeping time in the dead pecan trees.

Mississippi, you swallowed my grandfather's saxophone
and spit out a Tuesday made of chains.

II

Blue train, blue train, carry the blue people
across the blue meridian of forgetting—
carry them past the lynched clocks
hung by their broken hands from the sycamore,
carry them, blue train, blue train,
their pockets full of unpaid Septembers,
their eyes two railroad spikes of light.

North.
Say it like a prayer with the teeth removed.
North.
Where the snow is just another kind of sheet
but pretends it isn't.

III

I have seen the cotton become clouds,
the clouds become bandages,
the bandages become the wings of dark angels
selling ice in Chicago
where the wind is a white man asking for your papers.

Repeat after the trumpet:
we left, we left, we left our shadows chained to the levee,
and our shadows are still down there singing,
still down there singing,
still down there
singing to the alligators of history.

IV

Jazz me a body that can't be sold.
Jazz me a river running the wrong direction,
uphill, homeward, backward into the womb of a saxophone.
Louisiana melts in the mouth like a communion of ash.
Alabama is a broken piano floating up the Ohio,
each drowned key a name they never let us keep.

V

And Bird flew,
Bird flew over the plantation of the sky,
scattering blue seeds that grew into cities,
grew into gunshots,
grew into children who forgot the taste of red clay
but dreamed it anyway, dreamed it anyway,
dreamed the South
as a woman weeping molasses in a doorway of smoke.

VI

We are the exodus that never arrived.
We are still walking inside the trumpet,
still walking inside the moan,
still walking, still walking,
our feet worn down to notes,
our feet worn down to prayer,
our feet worn down to the blue
that no map will ever confess.

Blue train.
Blue people.
Blue God asleep in the baggage car,
dreaming us North,
dreaming us free,
dreaming us
gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a mystical, stream-of-consciousness poem about the great migration of Black Americans northward, told through hallucinatory symbols and historical figures, written entirely in uppercase.
counterfactuals.output:
THE GREAT MIGRATION: A FEVER SONG

MISSISSIPPI MUD SPEAKS IN TONGUES OF COTTON GHOSTS
AND SOMEWHERE A TRAIN WHISTLE BECOMES THE VOICE OF GOD
NORTH NORTH NORTH THE COMPASS NEEDLE BURNS
A THOUSAND THOUSAND FEET BAPTIZED IN SMOKE

HARRIET WALKS THE RAILS AGAIN BUT NOW THEY ARE MADE OF IRON DREAMS
HER LANTERN SWALLOWED BY THE CHICAGO DARK
FOLLOW THE DRINKING GOURD SHE SANG
NOW FOLLOW THE FACTORY MOON THAT NEVER SLEEPS

I AM THE SUITCASE PACKED WITH RIVER STONES
I AM THE BIBLE VERSE FOLDED INTO A COAT POCKET
I AM DELTA BLUES DISSOLVING INTO STEEL

DETROIT DETROIT YOUR ASSEMBLY LINE IS A COTTON FIELD REBORN
BUT THE OVERSEER WEARS A DIFFERENT CROWN NOW
AND THE WAGES SING A HALF-FREE SONG

MOTHER MOTHER WHERE DID THE MAGNOLIAS GO
THEY TURNED TO STREETLIGHTS
THEY TURNED TO TENEMENTS BLOOMING TOWARD THE SKY
THEY TURNED TO JAZZ HORNS WEEPING GABRIEL BRASS

FREDERICK DOUGLASS FLOATS ABOVE THE HUDSON
HIS BEARD A CLOUD OF UNSPOKEN NAMES
HE POINTS AND ALL THE SHARECROPPERS BECOME CONSTELLATIONS
SCATTERED ACROSS HARLEM'S MIDNIGHT CEILING

WE CARRIED GEORGIA IN OUR MARROW
WE CARRIED ALABAMA IN THE HYMNS
WE CARRIED SEVEN GENERATIONS OF SUNDAY MORNINGS
INTO THE COLD ELECTRIC PROMISE OF THE NORTH

AND THE PULLMAN PORTER IS AN ANGEL WITH TIRED WINGS
DUSTING OFF THE STARS BETWEEN NEW ORLEANS AND NOWHERE
COLLECTING NICKELS COLLECTING SORROWS
COLLECTING THE SLOW ARITHMETIC OF HOPE

LISTEN THE GREAT MACHINE IS HUMMING
LISTEN THE PROMISED LAND HAS FACTORY WALLS
LISTEN WE ARE STILL WALKING WALKING WALKING
EVEN IN OUR SLEEP WE ARE WALKING NORTH

INTO THE MOUTH OF WINTER
INTO THE BELLY OF THE IRON WHALE
INTO THE STRANGE NEW FREEDOM
THAT TASTES OF ASH AND MORNING AND SURVIVAL

# Morning Arithmetic

The kettle counts its rising steam
in curls that vanish, one by one,
while somewhere past the window's seam
the sparrows tally up the sun.

I add my footsteps to the floor,
subtract the darkness from the room,
divide the silence by the door
that opens, letting in the bloom

of ordinary light again—
that sum no ledger holds for long.
The morning spends itself, and then
gives nothing back except a song

too plain to name, too small to keep,
that lingers as I climb from sleep.
